passages.text: Unraveling Racial Disparities in Asthma Emergency Department Visits Using Electronic Healthcare Records and Machine Learning
Objective:

Hospital emergency department (ED) visits by asthmatics differ based on race and season. The objectives of tins study were to investigate season- and race-specific disparities for asthma risk, and to identify environmental exposure variables associated with ED visits among more than 42,000 individuals of African American (AAs) and European American (EAs) descent identified through electronic health records.
Methods:

We examined data from 42,375 individuals (AAs =14,491, EAs-27,884) identified in electronic health records (EHRs). We considered associated demographic (race, age, gender, insurance), clinical (smoking status, ED visits, FEV1%), and environmental exposures data (mold, pollen, pollutants). Machine learning techniques, including random forest (RF), extreme gradient boosting (XGB), and decision tree (DT) were used to build and identify race- and -season-specific predictive models for asthma ED visits.
Results:

Significant differences in ED visits and FEV1% among AAs and EAs were identified. ED visits by AAs was 32.0% higher than EA, and AAs had 6.4% lower FEV1% value than EAs. XGB model was used to accurately classify asthma patients visiting ED into AAs and EAs. Pollen factor and pollution (PM2.5, PM10) were the key variables for asthma in AAs and EAs, respectively. Age and cigarette smoking increase asthma risk independent of seasons.
Conclusions:

In this study, the observed racial and season-specific disparities between AAs and EAs asthmatics for ED visit and FEV1% severity, suggesting the need to address asthma disparities through key predictors including socio-economic status, particulate matter, and mold.
Graphical Abstract
INTRODUCTION

About 25 million people are affected by asthma in the United States of America. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, this translates to more than 14 million doctors’ office visits, two million emergency department visits, 500,000 hospitalizations per year and 3,564 death. Asthma costs the U.S. economy more than $82 billion annually in medical expenses, missed work and school days and deaths. The implementation of asthma clinical practice guidelines led to reduction in the overall mortality over the past three decades. However, African Americans (AAs) remain four times more likely to be hospitalized and seven times more likely to die from asthma compared to European American (EAs). Several factors, including socio-environmental risk factors (e.g., socio-economic status, insurance, education, traffic-related air pollution, mold, pollen, and cigarette smoke) are associated with increased asthma prevalence and decreased pulmonary function in children. However, how these risk factors differentially impact AAs from EAs is unknown.

Mining electronic health records (EHRs) provides an approach for rapidly generating large and diverse health-related databases without investing additional time and effort for collecting clinical data. Recently, several groups used a combination of EHR data and Twitter data to explore racial disparities in emergency department visits (EDs). The ED visit data modeled the frequency of asthmatic patients with the aid of machine learning algorithms. In this study, we analyzed patients’ demographic and socio-environmental exposure data along with EHR ED visit information to unravel racial disparities in asthma. These data may enhance a better understanding of health disparities and the development of intervention guidelines to improve the health of the minorities. We applied four machine learning algorithms to develop season- and race-specific statistical models for asthma ED visits/hospitalizations and severity and to identify the most-relevant socio-environmental exposure variables associated with hospital visits in AA and EA populations. To our knowledge no literature exists for season-and race-specific racial disparity models to predict asthma ED visits.
METHODS
Data sources
EHR clinical data:

University of Cincinnati is a major urban-based hospital located in the city of Cincinnati which is located in the Southwest Ohio and border to Kentucky (KY) in South and Indiana (IN) in West. The hospital primarily serves the resident of the Greater Cincinnati metropolitan area, which consists of urban, sub-urban and rural areas. EHR-based retrospective cohort study was conducted using the University of Cincinnati Medical Center EPIC database. The database contains de-identified clinical data for every individual, including visit dates, demographic characteristics, history of tobacco use, insurance type, and laboratory tests (in accordance with the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996). Demographic data including age, race, gender and clinical and laboratory data (FEV1%, ED visit, and smoking status) were obtained based on ICD 9/10 Codes (ICD-9: 493, ICD-10: J45) from November 1, 2012, to December 2017. European American (“White or Caucasian, n = 27,884”) and African American (“Black or African American, n = 14,491”) samples were included in the study. The sample represents the racial composition of the target population in the Cincinnati Metropolitan area. Figure 1 presents the general outline and workflow for EHR, clinical and environmental exposure datasets.
Ethics statement
The study protocol was approved by the Institutional Review Board (IRB) of University of Cincinnati (UC).
Environmental exposure data:

The air pollution data included particulate matter (PM2.5, PM10), carbon monoxide (CO), nitrogen dioxide (NO2), sulfur dioxide (SO2), and ozone. Daily air quality data for the Cincinnati metropolitan area were downloaded from the US EPA (https://www.epa.gov/outdoor-air-quality-data). Pollen (23 pollen types) and mold data (26 mold types) were obtained from Southwest Ohio Air Quality Agency based in Cincinnati using a Rotorod sampler. The data recorded as grains per cubic meter of air for pollen levels and spores per cubic meter of air for mold levels. The unit of measurement for pollen levels was pollen count/m3 and for mold levels it was mold count/m3.
Data integration

The de-identified EHR dataset extracted from the EPIC center was downloaded and merged with demographic data, smoking status, FEV1% measurement, and environmental allergen and exposure data based on the date of the occurrence via the Pandas software library for Python (http://pandas.pydata.org/). We linked daily hospitalization due to asthma with environmental data by date. Consecutive days of ED record were considered as a single visit. Patients with multiple smoking station record within the timeframe of the study were assigned to one of the four stati - ‘Current’ if at least one record of current smoking, ‘Former’ if the record showed a least one instance of former smoking but no instances of current smoking, ‘Passive’ if the records show passive or indirect/second hand smoking exposure only, and ‘Never’ status if no record of current, passive, or former smoking were observed.
Descriptive analysis

The dataset was split into AAs and EAs cohorts based on self-identified race information. Descriptive statistics summarized the patients’ clinical characteristics, ED visit frequency, air pollution, and pollen/mold data for each cohort. Numeric variables used mean, median, and standard deviation and categorical variables used the proportion or frequency. We assessed skewness of the continuous variables through histograms. To determine the difference between AA and EA, we conducted non-parametric Mann-Whitney U Test for the skewed variables, a two-sample t-test for normally distributed variables and the chi-square test for categorical data. The Mann–Whitney U test is more powerful test for testing the equality of distributions of two independent populations than the two-sample t-test when the distributions are heavy-tailed or very-skewed distributions. The correlation between environmental exposures variables were accessed using the Spearman’s rank correlation on stratified data based on meteorological seasons.
Racial disparity measurement

To determine racial disparity in particulate exposure and clinical values between AAs and EAs, we generated a disparity measure for each variable. For each variable, we calculated the mean disparity of AA population compared to EA population (differences in mean value). For each variable i,
Then, the percent disparity measure for AA is calculated as the mean disparity of AA relative to EA mean as follows:
For example, to compute the percent ED visit disparity, the ED visit frequency of each patient was calculated followed by the mean frequency visit for both AA and EA patient groups.
Seasonal patterns of environmental exposure and ED visit

We categorized ED visit data by meteorological seasons: winter (December, January, February), spring (March, April, May), summer (June, July, August), and fall (September, October, November). We determine seasonal differences in the number of ED visit in each racial group using chi-square test.
ED visit frequency and asthma severity

We classified patient’s ED visit frequency into quantiles with above and below the 3rd quartile labeled as “Frequent (F)” and “Infrequent (I)”, respectively. Additionally, for the severity of asthma, we used National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI) Guidelines of lung function using FEV1% to classify asthmatic patients into intermittent (I) if FEV1% ⩾ 80, moderate (M) if FEV1% 60-80, and severe (S) if FEV1% < 60, according to the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI) Guidelines.
Predictive model development

Race-and season-specific predictive classification models were developed for the two response variables (ED visit and asthma severity). Four different machine learning algorithms were used for building the predictive models with the season specific environmental exposures, demographic, and clinical variables as predictors (see the Supplemental Text for more detail). The best model for each racial category was identified.
Logistic regression (LR):

This model is the probability of a categorical response variable as a function of predictor variables. The fitted model generates a nonlinear logistic curve predicting the probability of the categorical response factor given the set of independent variables. LR provides estimate of odds ratio and their significance on predicting response class, based on which we can identify the best set of classifiers which are easy to interpret. For ED visit, the logistic regression model predicts the probability of frequent (F) and infrequent (I) visitor based on the combinations of predictors. Similarly, for the asthma severity class prediction, the LR model fit a multiclass model to predict the probability of each of the asthma severity class.
Decision Tree (DT):

This is a non-parametric supervised learning method of classification by constructing a hierarchical tree structure with edges and nodes based on the binary split of predictors. The procedure seeks the most informative variable or nodes to split the data into distinct groups that classify the response variable into the most homogeneous binary classes. Each possible value of the variables were tested for the split and the optimal split is determined by the impurity measure.
Random Forest (RF):

RF is a supervised classification method that uses an ensemble of decision tree created by using bootstrap samples of training data and random feature selection in the step of tree construction. By aggregating the prediction results across all trees in the forest, it provides improved predictive accuracy and better control of over-fitting.
Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGB):

XGB is a tree-based ensemble method designed to improve models by gradient descent through iteratively adding weak classifiers. A greedy approach is used for tree development while reducing overfitting.

Data preprocessing and filtering of variables with near zero variance was performed using R package healthcare.ai. Data was split into 60:40 for training and testing sets, respectively. To minimize model overfitting and prediction errors, we performed 10-fold cross validation. For the binary classification of ED visit and multiclass classification of asthma severity, area under the ROC curve and accuracy rate were used to evaluate the performance of the model, respectively.

For LR and DT, R package caret was used for the model building and prediction analysis. Both models were run under default setting of hyper-parameters. For DT, the caret package automatically determines the tree pruning and Gini impurity index to determine the split. The RF and XGB were run using healthcare.ai package with default setting. For both cases, the healthcase.ai package internally tuned to find best combination of hyper-parameters and select the best model with optimal ROC or accuracy rate. Finally, the performance of all modeling (for each race and for each season) were evaluated using the classification accuracy on the testing set.
Variable importance

Variable importance scores (VIS) were computed for each input variable under each predictive model described above. Using the LR, the variable importance score is the absolute standardized beta-coefficients (i.e. absolute t-statistics) from the model normalized from max = 100 to min = 0.

The DT, RF, and XGB models assign the Gini impurity index to each predictor variable as a measure of importance score with higher impurity index reflecting higher importance. The importance scores were scaled from max = 100 to min = 0. The contribution of each variable in classifying or predicting ED visit or asthma severity was ranked. The top 10 important variables for each race and season were presented.
RESULTS
Demographic variables

The EHR data set consisted of 42,375 patients, with frequent ED visits and multiple entries reported for the same patients during the study period (Table 1). 34.2% of the total patients were self-identified AA and 65.8% were self-identified EA. Further, 64.8% and 67.9% of the samples were females for AA and EA, respectively. The mean age of ED visit for AAs was 48.16 years (SD = 15.47), while the mean age of ED visit for EAs was 50.58 (SD = 21.12). The median ED visits were 7 and 6 for AA and EA, respectively. Smoking is more prevalent in AA with 41.93% AA vs 28.6% EA patients were current smoker (p-value < 2E-16). A plot of the distribution of FEV1% vs age and ED visits vs age is shown in Figure 2. In both races, ED visits increased with the age (rblack = 0.29, pblack < 2E-16; rwhite = 0.19, pblack < 2E-16), but the rate for AA is significantly higher than the rate for the EA (pdiff < 2E-16) . (Figure 2A). Age and FEV1% showed a mild but significant negative correlation (rblack = −0.15, pblack < 2E-16; rwhite = −0.17, pblack < 2E-16) in both black and white groups. In the younger age group (Age 18-29), whites had higher FEV1% than the black counterparts (82% vs. 96%, non-significance p-value = 0.13) but the difference is reduced as the age progress (Figure 2B).
Racial disparities in environmental exposure and clinical data

Figure 3 showed the racial disparities in environmental exposures (pollen, mold, air pollution), age, ED visit and FEV1% between AAs and EAs. The negative percent disparity measure of FEV1% showed that AA asthmatics had lower FEV1% compare to EA asthmatics. Similarly, AA were slightly younger than the EA as shown by the negative percent disparity for age. The ED visit had a positive mean percentage disparity which showed more frequent ED visits by AA asthmatics than the EAs. Sweetgum, boxelder, osage orange, linden, and ash were among the top pollens AA asthmatic patients were exposed in higher amount while ragweed, alder, and chestnut were among the top pollens exposure to EA asthmatic patients during the ED visit period (Figure 3). On the other hand, the disparity level between AA and EA was minimal for most of the pollution attributes (such as PM2.5, PM10, NO2) which suggested that both racial groups were similarly exposed to traffic air pollutions, nonetheless PM2.5, PM10, and SO2 were more exposed to AA than EA (Figure 3). Partly, racial disparities could be also associated to the neighborhood locations on the Greater Cincinnati Metropolitan area, which is a mix of urban, suburban and rural. Using zip code across the metropolitan area, we conducted an association between the population densities of non-Hispanic African American vs. the average PM2.5 and found a modest correlation r = 0.558 (p-value = 5.98e-8)

Figure 4 showed the difference in the ED visit was statistically significance and so was the FEV1%, age, and multiple pollen and molds. Difference in categorical data were accessed using the chi-square test whereas a two-sample t-test (normally distributed variables) or the Mann-Whitney U test (for skewed variables) was used for the comparison of numeric variables. Normality was accessed using histogram plots (Appendix Figure 1). Even though the percent disparity of pollution exposure was low, the difference was statistically significance (adj. p-value < 0.05) except for the NO2 which was not significantly different (Figure 4).
Distribution of exposure variables

The distribution of air pollutants over the study seasons were relatively stable except for ozone, whose levels were highest in summer and lowest in winter (Appendix Figure 2A). In particular, pollens were season specific, such as ragweed in Fall, sycamore in Spring and so on, and higher quantities of molds were observed during summer (Appendix Figure 2B, 2C). For both EA and AA asthmatic patients, the highest number of ED visits occurred in July/August and December/January while March/April had the least number of ED visits (Appendix Table 1, Appendix Figure 2D),).Spring showed the most widespread correlation across different variables while during summer, the correlation was observed mainly in blocks (Appendix Figure 3). Molds and pollution showed correlation during fall and winter (Appendix Figure 3C, D). Significant p-value was observed between AA and EA in FEV1%, age, gender, and smoking status. Also, significant differences were observed in pollution between AAs and EAs (Figure 4). Ragweed exhibited the strongest difference between AA and EA.
Season- and race- specific prediction models

Variation in the environmental exposures could explain the racial disparities observed in AA and EA asthmatic patients. To identify the important exposure variables associated with the race-specific ED visits and asthma severity, we performed classification analysis using multiple predictive models (see details in Method section and Supplementary Text). Since the contributions of pollen and molds are season-specific, the classification was performed independently for winter, spring, summer, and fall. For both races and all four seasons, XGB performed best with high prediction accuracy rate (Fig 5A). In particular, the prediction accuracies under XGB model for AAs were 0.94, 0.98, 0.97, and 0.97 during winter, spring, summer, and fall, respectively. Similar high prediction accuracy was observed for EA classification (Figure 5A, Table 2). Similarly, XGB model was the best performing model for asthma severity measures followed by RF, DT and LR (Fig 5B). Random forest was only the best performing model for AA in winter with an accuracy rate of 0.50, followed by XGB with an accuracy rate of 0.48. The accuracy rates for both XGB and RF were statistically significant for all 4 seasons and both races (Figure 5B, Table 3).
Season- specific variable importance selection

XGB, the best performing model, was used to assess the VIS (variable importance score) in each race across seasons. Appendix Figure 4 shows the season-specific top 10 variables from the XGB models for both races for ED visit classification. In winter, the mold factor was the most important variable for both AA and EA. Additionally, several pollution variables such as CO, Ozone, NO2, and SO2 were also identified as important variables (Appendix Figure 4A). In spring, molds such as drechslera, stemphylium, fusarium, and tolura were the top predictors for both AA and EA cohorts. Among the pollens, birch and alder were prominent among AA, while alder, cedar juniper, and hackberry were the top predictors among the EA patients (Appendix Figure 4B). In summer, pine, ragweed, and aspergillus were the top 3 exposure variables for both AA and EA as well as grasses, elm, torula, massarina, and aspergillus were among the top 10 predictors for both cohorts (Appendix Figure 4C). During the fall, grasses and massarina were the top predictors for AA and EA, respectively (Appendix Figure 4D). For asthma severity, age was identified as the top predictor variable across all seasons for both races. Smoking status, gender, SO2, NO2, CO, and ascospores were among the top 10 important variables in all seasons (Appendix Figure 5A–D).
DISCUSSION

In this study, we used a large EHR dataset from 2012-2015 with over 42,000 patients to systematically investigate race disparities in asthma. By using mold, pollen, air pollutions, clinical and demographic variables, we identified key season-specific environmental exposures contributing to racial disparities of asthma ED visit in AA and EAs. We also showed that environmental exposure variables were highly correlated with ED visit frequency. We compared the performance of four different machine learning algorithm with XGB as the best performer. XGB revealed the most important variables that contribute to racial disparities in ED visit with a 92%+ accuracy rate in predicting frequent vs. infrequent ED visitor in both races and across all seasons. Pollens were the most environmental important variables for ED visit prediction in except in winter. In winter, molds (epicoccum, ascospores) and pollutants (CO, Ozone, SO2, PM10) were the most important predictors for both AA and EA, which could be due to the fact that pollens are mostly absent in the winter. In general, pollen and molds were important risk factor for asthmatics in spring while grasses were important in summer and fall (Appendix Figure 4).

In addition to ED visits, we used FEV1% severity measure (intermittent, moderate, and severe) to cluster asthmatic individuals in the EHR system. Severe and intermittent asthmatics were distinguished at higher accuracy in AAs than EAs. For both AAs and EAs, age was the most significant contributor to asthma severity. This study showed a negative correlation between age and severity of asthma and positive correlation between age and ED visit in both AAs and EA population. These results were supported by previous studies that showed a strong and negative correlation between age and FEV1%. and frequent ED visit for younger AA. Although insurance type is significantly associated with race, race stratified analysis didn’t show insurance as an important asthma risk predictor for either race. Smoking status and pollution exposures were among the top predictor of asthma severity in both races across all seasons (Appendix Figure 5). Existing literature corroborates our findings that smoking is a major factor that exacerbates asthma. The risk of having asthma increased with smoking in AAs.. Numerous studies have reported the association between air pollution and asthma. Multiple studies have linked exposure to PM2.5 to asthma development exacerbations in adults. A recent study estimates that 8-12% of asthma ED visits worldwide could be attributed to ozone and 4-9% to PM2.5. Traffic pollution derived diesel particles represent a major source of PM2.5 in large urban centers and have been linked to increased susceptibility to asthma development and exacerbations. Our study showed that there was a modest positive racial disparity in the exposure of PM10, and Ozone, negative disparity for FEV1%, and higher rate of current smokers in AA. The cumulative effect of such adverse factors might have resulted more frequent asthma exacerbation in AA patients and the higher racial disparities of ED visit. Our analysis further identified certain pollens such as sweetgum and boxelder associated to positive disparity in AA while other pollens such as ragweed, alder, hackberry, sycamore and others were associated to positive disparity in EA. Distribution of tree types across different neighborhood in the greater Cincinnati area might have played the role in such selective disparity in pollen types, even though their effects in the asthma exacerbation across the racial group is unknown. However, our results highlight the racial difference in exposure of pollens and molds that need further consideration.

Our analysis revealed that the population exposures ranked higher in the importance measure of asthma severity for AA in the winter while during the rest of the seasons, pollution factors ranked slightly higher for EA than AA (Appendix Figure 5). This could be due to the neighbor location of AA and EA, where AA residency are located closer to the highways and roads in the urban center and lack efficient clean air circulation. In the winter, the cold weather may have caused the pollution to accumulate to the residency in the close proximal of roads and highway, and thus affecting AA patients. The environment is a key factor in human health, and seasonal changes in particular have been associated with human conditions and diseases including allergies. For example, mortality rates in the U.S. show a notable seasonality with rates in winter 25% higher than in summer. The results of our study have important implications in healthcare and highlight the value of considering seasonality when assessing population wide health risk and management.

AAs had more frequent ED visits with an average of 32% higher than EAs’ ED visits. Previous studies have shown that AAs are less likely to visit their primary care physician compared to the EAs, which could lead to frequent ED visits.; . Additionally, AA asthmatic had lower FEV1% than EA which could lead to more asthma exacerbation and consequently frequent ED visits by AA asthmatic patients. Such frequent and unplanned ED visits create more economic burden on the patient as well as the healthcare system.;  Similar to our findings, others had reported a significant correlation between mold counts and asthma-related ED visits. Recent studies have suggested that climate changes can cause season-specific increase in fungal spore production for some mold types, which in turn could worsen asthma severity in susceptible patients. For example, an increase in average daily temperature was associated with an increase in cladosporium counts over an 8-year study period conducted in Denver, CO, USA.

It is important to note that our analyses, and hence interpretations, are subject to several limitations. Firstly, the patients’ race in EHRs is self-reported, which ignore the possibility that individuals have mixed racial ancestry and group individual in a single racial category. Access and collection of biological data such as genetic information can produce a better classification of a patient’s racial ancestry and overcome this limitation. Secondly, users request for a daily number of ED visits with a primary diagnosis of asthma and ICD-9/ICD-10 codes. However, defining asthma on the basis of primary diagnosis and ICD-9/ICD-10 codes could potentially lead to misclassification, although previous studies showed that such misclassification could not affect the overall interpretation of big data like ours (42,357 records). Third, our analysis assume an accurate FEV1% measurement in the EHR which is dependent on an accurate manual measurement of EHR staff. Inadvertently measurement error by EHR staff due to the ED structure could affect the results. Although we do not have skin test sensitivity between AA and EA specific to this study, multiple studies showed that Black individuals are more likely to have at least 1 positive skin prick test compared with white individuals. Finally, this study relied solely on structured data captured in the electronic health record. Study findings are therefore subject to the accuracy and completeness of electronic documentation by the EHR team.

Regardless of these limitations, our study has key strengths. We used an exhaustive list of mold species (n=23), pollen types (n=26), air pollution data (PM2.5, PM10, CO, NO2, SO2, and ozone), lung function tests (FEV1%), ED visits, insurances, and smoking information to investigate asthma disparities between AA and EA asthmatics. With the increasing availability of scalable computational models, opportunities to apply EHR data to clinical decision-making are emerging. The use of ML algorithms allowed us to calculate the most important variables and determine which race-specific environmental factors are important contributors to asthma ED visits. In addition, significant progress has been made by US initiatives (Electronic Medical Records and Genomics (eMERGE), BioVU, Million Veteran Program (MVP), and All Of Us  to improve the use of EHR by the research community.
Conclusion

In this study, we developed XGB model for asthma racial disparities in AA compared with EA using EHR demographic and clinical and environmental exposure datasets. Compared with AAs, EAs have lower asthma morbidity due to environmental exposure as reflected by lower asthma severity measure (FEV1%). In summary, we showed that EHR, in combination with publicly available environmental exposure data and machine learning methods, can provide a better insight into racial disparities in asthma.

Schematic representation of the workflow for clinical, and socio-environmental exposure datasets.

We used Python, a computer programming language, to program a data merging routine. We used Pandas, a python code package, to run Python code. We then used R, a statistical coding language, within R Studio, for asthma severity classification and ED Visit frequency. The previous steps were followed by machine learning algorithms through R packages (caret, Healthcare.ai), to produce the predictive models and prioritize the best predictive model. Finally, the most important variables that contributed to the best performing model were used for prediction. This pipeline is applied for both African American and European American datasets.
